narrative.text: A blank page with no extracted text.
Lists the editors of the Chinese edition of the Casebook on ethical issues in international health research, together with its two translators.

The copyright and cataloguing page of the Chinese edition of the WHO Casebook on ethical issues in international health research, published by People's Medical Publishing House with WHO's permission, with ISBN and printing details.

Acknowledgements for the research ethics casebook, crediting the WHO–University of Geneva research ethics training programme, its funder and the many people who contributed cases, ran online discussions and reviewed the text. Named reviewers came from around the world and gave feedback on the teaching guide and cases.
Continues the acknowledgements, thanking those who provided editorial, design and photographic support, signed by the four editors in March 2009.

The foreword to the casebook by WHO's Assistant Director-General for information, evidence and research, stressing that ethical standards are central to health research. It notes WHO's work on research ethics review and training and the need for local capacity in low-resource settings. It explains that the book uses real cases rather than prescriptive rules.

Gives biographies of the casebook's editors, describing their careers in international health research and bioethics. They include a Harvard expert who ran early oral rehydration trials, a Harvard professor of population health ethics, the head of WHO's research ethics review committee and a law professor who was WHO's first ethics director.

The first page of the casebook's table of contents, listing the introduction, teaching guide and chapters 1 and 2 with their case titles, from SARS and airline passengers to compassionate intervention in observational research.
The table of contents continued, listing chapters 3 on harm and benefit and 4 on voluntary informed consent, with case titles and cross-references.
The table of contents continued, listing chapters 5 on standard of care, 6 on obligations to participants and communities and 7 on privacy and confidentiality, with case titles.
The table of contents continued, listing the remaining privacy cases, chapter 8 on professional ethics, the glossary, suggested readings and appendix.
A section title page for the introduction.

Introduces the casebook of 64 real cases on ethical problems in planning, reviewing and conducting health research, aimed at researchers and ethics committees in international studies. It explains its use in teaching and that names and details were altered. It also begins describing WHO's background role in research.

Explains the rising concern over ethical issues as research grows more complex and international, and the potential for harm to vulnerable groups. It describes WHO's ethics review committee and its training work. It also notes how the cases grew out of a decade of Harvard and WHO workshops that found case discussion avoids imposing cultural bias.
A section title page for the teaching guide.

Introduces the teaching guide, explaining that case-based teaching differs from lecturing and relies on facilitating structured discussion. It describes how facilitators, not students, should use the book, with permission to copy cases for non-commercial teaching.

Explains the facilitator's role in case-based learning, shifting focus from lecturer to participants, and stresses that cases have no simple answers. Using the example of treating TB found in HIV vaccine trial screening, it warns against steering learners toward the facilitator's own view.

Suggests further questions for discussing the TB treatment example, drawing on CIOMS guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. It then advises course organisers on selecting cases and choosing whether to start sessions with a case or a lecture. Citations to CIOMS and Helsinki are given.

Compares starting sessions with a case or with a lecture and recommends small groups of six to eight for large classes. It advises anticipating responses and challenging views the facilitator agrees with as well as those it does not. It then begins a list of practical tips for leading discussion.

Continues practical tips for leading group discussion, such as involving everyone, treating all equally, rephrasing points from second-language speakers, avoiding personal attacks and periodically summarising.

Begins the guide to exploring each chapter's content, explaining that chapter introductions can be shared with learners. It poses questions for chapter 1 on why research must be distinguished from medical care and public health practice. It also asks what patients need to know before joining a study.

Continues the questions for chapter 1 on informed consent, vulnerability and whether participation by patients with no other access to care is voluntary. It suggests using the chapter to introduce the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS guidelines and to train ethics committee members on their remit.

Turns to chapter 2 on study design, noting that even scientifically sound designs, such as deceptive social psychology experiments or sponsor-favoured designs, raise ethical issues. It poses questions on scientific validity, placebo controls and equipoise. It lists readings including a WHO/TDR review and an Oxford casebook.

Continues the study design questions on deception, low-burden designs, unjust exclusion of groups, testing traditional remedies and whether research must meet national priorities. It then introduces chapter 3 on harm and benefit and the difficulty of weighing risks in developing countries.

Continues the chapter 3 guidance on benefits for families, communities and countries and on undue inducement, citing microbicide trial debates and a US bioethics commission report. It then introduces chapter 4 on informed consent, noting that participants often misunderstand studies and that consent forms should not simply be exported.

Continues the informed consent guidance, questioning whether the term itself is ambiguous and suggesting separate terms for disclosure and comprehension. It raises issues of community leaders or husbands deciding for others, sensitivity in violence-against-women research, literacy and capacity.

Introduces chapter 5 on standard of care and the debate over a single universal standard versus local standards in multisite trials, recommending a Nuffield Council report. It poses questions on whether giving controls only the local standard is exploitative and when cheaper, less effective interventions may be tested.

Continues the standard-of-care questions, asking whether testing less effective interventions is ethical and when developing-country committees may approve trials unacceptable elsewhere. It then introduces chapter 6 on obligations to participants and communities, pointing to guidance on care in vaccine trials and ancillary care.

Lists examples of obligations owed to participants, such as to those harmed by research. It then introduces chapter 7 on privacy and confidentiality, citing an article on public health and data protection. It asks whether confidentiality has limits when researchers learn of illegal or dangerous behaviour.

Lists situations that test the limits of confidentiality, such as child abuse, notifiable infections and illegal abortion, and asks how best to protect privacy in stigmatised groups and stored data. It then raises questions for chapter 8 on conflicts of interest and scientific misconduct.
Ends the teaching guide with questions on who should identify scientific misconduct and lists supplementary resources for case-based teaching, such as notes on the Tuskegee syphilis study case.
A section title page for the case studies.
The title page of chapter 1, on defining research.

Introduces chapter 1 on when ethics committee approval is needed, defining research involving human subjects as systematic activity aimed at new knowledge. It explains that the main purpose of research is to gain knowledge rather than to benefit individual patients, even with innovative treatment.

Notes that not all research tests new interventions and that government surveys can blur the line with research. It stresses that the search for knowledge must not override human welfare, citing past abuses. It discusses how to handle conflicts between science and participant protection, such as viral challenge studies.

Describes the Nuremberg Code's insistence on consent and the creation of independent research ethics committees after unethical studies. It discusses their remit and limits, noting that operations research is not always low-risk. It also gives examples of how such research may create inequities or expose staff responsible for poor decisions.

Explains that research ethics committees lack jurisdiction over public health surveillance, where other mechanisms balance individual and population interests, creating grey areas when research questions are added to routine activities. It lists recommended readings on defining research, including a BMJ article on audit versus research.

Case 1, on SARS and airline passengers, describes a national centre in country X tracing contacts of SARS cases on flights in 2003 using passenger lists and local health agencies. It asks whether the data collection was surveillance, prevention or research and whether ethics approval and consent were needed.

Case 2 describes an institute evaluating donor-funded adolescent HIV testing, antenatal care and condom education programmes in several regions, which it claimed were low-risk operations research exempt from ethics review. Questions ask which activities are research and what low risk means.

Case 3 describes an Asian neurosurgeon who injected olfactory ensheathing cells from aborted fetuses into more than 500 patients with ALS, Parkinson's disease, stroke and paralysis, claiming benefits. He refuses a sham-controlled trial urged by supporters as unethical. The case asks whether this is therapy or research.

Lists the questions for the neurosurgeon case: whether it is innovative therapy, an experiment or research, whether a placebo-controlled trial would be unethical, how efficacy could be shown and who should oversee doctors.

Case 4 of the Chinese edition of the casebook on ethical issues in international health research describes a university team hurriedly studying the health of an isolated indigenous community in South America, recently contacted by farmers and forestry workers, using a household survey and blood tests. It notes the researchers also saw a chance to study the group's genetics, and ends with questions on harms, benefits to the community and duties towards a sick child.
A divider page for Chapter 2, on issues in study design.

Opens the Chapter 2 introduction on scientifically and ethically sound study design, asking whether the scientific quality of a protocol is an ethical matter and whether research ethics committees are the right bodies to judge it. It argues that exposing participants to harm is justified only by expected benefits to society or to participants, so poor design raises ethical concerns. Hypothetical variations on disease severity illustrate how competing values must be weighed.

Discusses who should assess science during ethics review, separating pure scientific evaluation, ethical evaluation of methods and the judgement of whether better science justifies extra burdens on participants. It treats the last two as core tasks of ethics committees. It then turns to the use of placebo controls, quoting the CIOMS guideline that control groups should generally receive a proven effective intervention.

Continues the discussion of placebo controls, citing the Declaration of Helsinki and listing why different parties favour placebos, including sponsors' interests and settings where effective treatment is unavailable locally. It presents clinical equipoise as one way to justify placebo designs. The page then introduces so-called natural experiments, using the example of people without malaria immunity moving to endemic lowlands.

Discusses the inclusion of women and children in research, noting that their past exclusion as vulnerable groups left little evidence on safe treatment for them, with a footnote citing UNAIDS/WHO guidance on HIV prevention trials. It also cautions committees about possible coercion and introduces a second design issue concerning the purpose of research.

Explains that controlled trials expose a few people to risk so that reliable knowledge can benefit many, which implies participants should come from populations able to benefit from the results. It raises the specific concern of sponsors from developed countries testing drugs in developing countries where the product may not later be available, and stresses that research should respond to host country needs. A list of recommended reading begins.

Continues the recommended reading list for Chapter 2, with summaries of articles on including desperate volunteers in randomized trials, ethical challenges of study design and consent in resource-poor settings, and the meaning of uncertainty and clinical equipoise.

Case 5 describes a study in a South-East Asian country tracking how many seriously ill children under five are referred from primary care to hospital under WHO and UNICEF's Integrated Management of Childhood Illness strategy, and their outcomes. It outlines the follow-up methods and asks whether the researchers' presence creates obligations to help families or health workers with referral.
The end of Case 5, asking whether researchers should give money or other help for child referrals, with a credit to the original case authors at Johns Hopkins.

Case 6 describes an anthropologist's study in a West African country of how women who sell sex negotiate condom use, in which research assistants pose as clients and a second assistant intervenes before any sex occurs. It notes the ethics committee approved the deceptive design but a journal later objected, and poses questions on alternatives, publication and reporting results to participants.
The end of Case 6, asking what problems could arise when communicating results to the participants, with a reference on confidentiality in fieldwork.

Case 7 describes a researcher at an infectious disease hospital in South-East Asia who plans to send men posing as villagers to ask drug sellers what they recommend for a child with diarrhoea, without disclosure. It asks whether the drug sellers had a right to know they were research subjects, whether intervention or debriefing is required, and how risks compare with benefits.

Case 8 explains the burden of hepatitis B and the difference between plasma-derived and recombinant vaccines, then describes a placebo-controlled infant trial of a new vaccine in a city where vaccine coverage was below 20%. It begins posing questions on whether a placebo arm is ethical when most local children have no other access to vaccination.
The end of Case 8, asking how the trial could be improved to meet ethical standards and whether consent from one parent is sufficient.

Case 9 describes an older placebo-controlled trial of TB prevention with isoniazid and multidrug regimens in HIV-positive people in Africa, explaining TB risk in HIV and the role of isoniazid. It outlines the trial design, with oral consent and at least three years of follow-up. Questions ask whether the placebo was justified and how a placebo differs ethically from no treatment.
The end of Case 9, asking whether the trial should have been conducted in Africa given the higher cost of multidrug regimens, with a credit to the original case authors.

Case 10 describes the malaria burden and the push for a vaccine, then sets out a planned vaccine trial among children under five in remote villages with few health workers or facilities. It explains that the trial would randomly select children from a community health database. Children would receive vaccine or placebo after household visits to explain the study and obtain consent.

Explains that the malaria vaccine trial would use deaths as its endpoint and make no other intervention, even though low-cost measures could prevent nearly all malaria deaths in the study population. Questions ask about the researchers' obligations and about the role and capacity of host-country ethics review when US review has already taken place.

Case 11 describes clinic records at a large South African hospital showing much higher STI rates among people identifying as coloured than as black, even after adjusting for socioeconomic status, and the country's history of racial classification. A researcher wants to study this, but a colleague wants race questions removed for fear of stigma, and the case asks who is right.
The end of Case 11, asking whether politically constructed racial categories should be used in research and whether clinic records alone justify the study hypothesis.

Case 12 recounts the controversy over placebo-controlled trials of short-course AZT to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission in Africa and Asia, with a footnote on WHO infant feeding advice. It gives the arguments for a placebo control, such as no local treatment being available and the long regimen being impractical. It then introduces the mainly Western critics who argued for an active control.

Sets out critics' arguments that the AZT trials should have used the long-course regimen as control, citing the Declaration of Helsinki and double standards. Questions ask whether sponsor ethics committees should still insist on the long regimen and whether such trials imply double standards.

Case 13 describes a trial in India comparing the herbal Ayurvedic preparation Ayush-64 with the standard chloroquine regimen for vivax malaria, with footnotes explaining chloroquine resistance, malaria species and Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. It sets out the eligibility criteria and written consent process. Eligible patients were then randomly assigned to one of the two treatments.

Details the treatment and follow-up schedules for the Ayush-64 and chloroquine-primaquine arms, including rescue treatment for non-responders and no follow-up of dropouts. Questions ask what evidence justifies testing a traditional remedy in humans, whether the study is ethical and what is owed to those who withdraw.

Case 14 describes a researcher's proposal to test a popular, cheap South Asian traditional remedy for bloody diarrhoea, based on the plant Hydrocotyle asiatica, which has never been clinically studied or chemically characterized. The review committee hesitated to approve it, and the researcher accused opponents of Western bias against traditional medicine. Questions ask whether the committee's assessment was right and what alternative design it might suggest.
The end of Case 14, asking whether the charge of Western bias is fair, whether approval would imply double standards, and how disagreements between researchers and committees should be resolved.

Case 15 describes a planned population-based twin study in a South-East Asian country with high rates of suicide and alcohol dependence, involving 2000 twin pairs and 1000 single-born people interviewed about common mental disorders and life adversity. Questions concern whether simply referring people with mental disorders, without ensuring treatment or follow-up, is adequate, and what is owed to identical twins with serious illness.

Case 16 describes an observational study of newborn care practices in a South-East Asian community with very high neonatal mortality, in which field workers are told only to observe and not intervene. When a field worker sees potentially harmful practices, such as overly diluted infant food, the case asks whether she should intervene, how the design could avoid the dilemma and whether others in the home must consent.

Case 17 describes a field worker in an East Asian newborn observation study who sympathizes with families and is asked to help a child with a high fever two days into illness, the nearest clinic being 20 kilometres away. Questions ask whether her personal duty to help outweighs her duty to the study and how she should handle further requests.
A divider page for Chapter 3, on harms and benefits.

Opens the Chapter 3 introduction on whether research benefits and harms are fairly distributed, noting that research raises ethical concern because scientists' needs do not always match participants' interests. It discusses justice in selecting participants when a study offers benefits to more people than it can enrol. It then notes the lack of guidance on how ethics committees should balance competing considerations.

Explains that in early drug trials participants may face harm or discomfort without expecting benefit, and that ethics committees must minimize harms, ensure benefits outweigh them and see that consent is fully informed. It then discusses the difficulty of comparing uncertain harms and benefits that affect different people differently. Examples include the question of testing a new vaccine in younger adolescents who can assent but not consent.

Raises harms that fall on people beyond participants, such as unknown viruses from xenotransplantation, genetic findings affecting relatives, and stigma for a whole town in South Asian HIV research. A recommended reading list follows, summarizing articles on the exclusion of older people from studies, community engagement and scientific imperialism.
The end of the Chapter 3 reading list, summarizing a BMJ editorial on whether research in poor countries that benefits patients in rich countries is exploitative.

Case 18 explains that rotavirus causes severe childhood diarrhoea worldwide, with most of about 527 000 annual deaths in low-income countries, so vaccination matters everywhere. It describes a country weighing the risk of intussusception linked to a vaccine against rotavirus deaths and deciding to vaccinate all infants if affordable. The health ministry instructs a state-owned drug company to obtain the technology from the North American manufacturer.

Describes how the North American company refused to transfer rotavirus vaccine technology, citing recovery of development costs and liability, and notes the option of compulsory licensing under the WTO TRIPS agreement, explained in a footnote. Questions ask whether the vaccine should be used given intussusception risk and what level of risk is acceptable.

Case 19 describes a trial in Africa of a pneumococcal vaccine for children, in which 90% of vaccinated children stayed free of disease after three years. Some scientists wanted to withhold vaccine from the control group afterwards to study longer-term effects, but all controls were vaccinated, and the questions ask whether withholding could ever be justified.

Case 20 describes a randomized trial of a drug to prevent breast cancer recurrence that a data safety monitoring board recommended stopping after three years because of a strong but not statistically significant trend favouring treatment. It asks about the role of such boards and when researchers may set aside statistical significance for moral reasons.

Case 21, on pregnancy in health research, describes a multi-country trial of a vaginal microbicide for HIV prevention among women at high risk in Africa and South Asia, which excluded pregnant women because fetal safety was unknown. Researchers found that many women paused participation for pregnancy and returned within three months, apparently after miscarriage or abortion. The case then outlines how far abortion is legal and safely available in each study country.

The end of Case 21, with questions on what researchers and sponsors should do about participants seeking possibly unsafe abortions, whether to warn about this risk, and whether such trials should run where safe abortion is not available.

Case 22 recounts 1990s research on non-surgical female sterilization with quinacrine pellets inserted into the uterus, with a footnote on the drug's history. It explains why non-surgical methods were sought given high maternal mortality and poor access to surgery. Despite conflicting safety evidence and criticism from women's advocacy groups, scientists at a research institute planned programmes to provide it.

The end of Case 22, giving the scientists' view that denying women a cheap, easy sterilization method would be unethical, and asking whether quinacrine use is justified if it may cause cancer, whether unregistered drugs should be exported, and whether the scientists' conduct was misconduct.
A divider page for Chapter 4, on voluntary informed consent.

Opens the Chapter 4 introduction on whether consent to research is voluntary and informed and given by competent people. Citing consent before the Nuremberg Code, it quotes the Code's first principle, which requires legal capacity, free choice without coercion or deceit, and enough understanding of the nature, duration, purpose, methods and risks of the experiment.

Explains that the Nuremberg Code makes consent a personal duty of each researcher and the starting point of research ethics, and identifies three elements of valid consent: capacity, voluntariness and adequate, understandable information. It discusses the legal and cognitive dimensions of capacity. It also notes the challenge of patients confusing treatment with research and feeling obliged to take part.

Discusses the difficulty ethics committees face in applying voluntariness, since strict limits can exclude poor populations or bar needed medical services as undue inducement, and outlines committees' options. It then turns to the information element of consent, describing what must be disclosed for potential participants to decide. Footnotes cite the CIOMS guidelines.

Explains that informed consent serves to protect people from harms greater than they accept and partly shifts responsibility to participants, while researchers remain responsible for their welfare. It then discusses studies involving deception, distinguishing withholding information from giving misleading information. It begins to illustrate this with Case 7, in which assistants posed as customers of drug sellers.

Asks whether deceptive research like the drug seller study could be acceptable with full debriefing, noting CIOMS guidance that ethics committees should decide. It discusses low-risk studies where individual consent is impractical or too costly, and situations where some people, such as husbands in WHO-guided studies of violence against women, are not asked for consent. It stresses that consent is a process that often begins before a protocol is written.

Describes consent as a process that may include community consultation, meetings and time to consult family, with signing only the final step, and possibly renewed consent at later visits. It asks when consent requirements are met. A recommended reading list follows, including work on informed consent in HIV vaccine trials.

Continues the Chapter 4 reading list, summarizing papers on legal and ethical bases of informed consent in HIV vaccine trials, ethical challenges in resource-poor settings and community engagement in genetic variation research. Each entry gives a short description and web link.

Case 23 describes a double-blind trial in a West African country of periodic high-dose vitamin A for children aged 6 months to 5 years, in a village governed by a traditional chief and council of elders who held a festive community meeting to introduce the study. Questions ask whether the chief and elders can consent for the community and how important individual consent is here.

Case 24 describes a proposed randomized trial in an Asian country comparing ovarian removal plus tamoxifen with observation after surgery for premenopausal breast cancer, with footnotes on the treatments. The researchers argue that a placebo trial is impossible in the United States but that adjuvant treatment is rarely used locally. They propose omitting disclosure of uncertainty and randomization, arguing that local patients expect doctors to decide.

Explains that the researchers consulted South Asian women abroad, local women's federation officials and local doctors, who agreed that disclosing randomization was inappropriate. Questions ask whether cultural differences justify a different consent process and whether such trials are justified in poor countries.

Case 25 introduces a phase II trial of a non-contraceptive vaginal microbicide to protect women against HIV and other STIs, with footnotes defining microbicides and trichomoniasis. A North American organization and a host-country medical university run the study in two family planning clinics, funding new equipment and extra staff. Before it starts, the researchers meet potential participants at the clinics to explain the study.

Sets out the microbicide trial's eligibility rules, consent through an interpreter without involving sexual partners, and monthly clinic visits with STI testing, counselling and free condoms. Questions include what a community health committee can do if it disagrees, and whether it is ethical not to give HIV results when antiretroviral therapy is not available.

Case 26 describes an 11-year trial at an East Asian cancer hospital of radiotherapy after surgery for oesophageal cancer, conducted without ethics review and without telling patients they were in a trial, since researchers feared distrust of research. A journal published the paper alongside a critical editorial without informing the authors, and the questions concern these choices.

Case 27 describes a South Asian trial of vitamin A or beta-carotene supplements for pregnant women, randomized by community, with footnotes on beta-carotene and teratogens. It explains that maternal vitamin A deficiency is linked to preterm birth and infant death and outlines the trial's follow-up of mothers and babies. After about three months, some women complained to the village head about continuing the weekly intervention.

Describes women's complaints that the supplement was a Western drug with no real effect and their wish to stop the trial, then asks whether community randomization raises ethical issues and whether the consent process was adequate.

Case 28, based on 1990s research, describes a study of breastfeeding and mother-to-child HIV transmission, with a footnote on WHO infant feeding advice. It introduces an HIV-positive pregnant woman with two healthy children who received a blood transfusion during her last delivery. Following the protocol, she is told about the benefits of breastfeeding and the risk of transmission, and her doctor advises her to consider alternatives.

Describes how the HIV-positive woman decided to breastfeed and stay in the study, while her husband objected, claiming an equal say and threatening a court order, partly to keep receiving free infant formula. Questions ask whether partners should consent, what role the husband should have, whether free services are an undue inducement and how the risk-benefit balance could be improved.

Case 29 describes South American researchers building a dengue mouse model by reconstituting immune-deficient mice with human umbilical cord blood donated by about 100 women near delivery. One donor later insisted on withdrawing all her samples, which had been anonymized and injected into mice, and the case asks whether she was properly informed and whether her request is reasonable.

Case 30 describes a country allowing embryos up to 14 days old to be used for stem cell research, where fertility doctors obtain consent to donate surplus embryos on the same form as consent for assisted reproduction. It asks whether the word research can be dropped from the form, whether one form is acceptable, and how to obtain consent for future unspecified research.

Case 31 describes a survey with a European university of health practices and needs among older people in a formerly nomadic community north of the Sahara, in which researchers first sought permission from adult sons as heads of household. During one interview an 80-year-old man became ill, and his angry son accused the researchers of making him sick and told them to leave; questions ask how this could be avoided and what is special about research with older people.
A divider page for Chapter 5, on the standard of care.

Opens the Chapter 5 introduction on whose standard of care should apply in randomized trials in developing countries, citing paragraph 32 of the 2008 Declaration of Helsinki on placebo use. It explains that, under this view, the best proven intervention must be given to control groups unless there are compelling scientific reasons for a placebo. It then notes that commentators see two ways of applying the principle that ought implies can.

Sets out interpretations of the Helsinki provision, from banning studies where the best care cannot be given to comparing new interventions with the best treatment available locally. It describes the single global standard position, which rejects double standards. It also covers the highest attainable or sustainable local standard, which can justify testing low-cost alternatives against placebo where the prevailing standard is no treatment.

Notes criticism that sustainability is a political judgement and varies between countries, then describes the minimal view that participants should receive at least the standard of care prevailing in the study area. It raises questions about obligations to treat other conditions found during research, and notes that many argue researchers bear some responsibility for participants' wellbeing.

Argues that researchers and sponsors from wealthy countries carry greater responsibility in poor countries and can help raise local standards of care through partnerships before research begins. A recommended reading list follows, summarizing articles on clinical research ethics in developing countries and the US FDA response to revisions of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Case 32, based on 1990s research, describes a Northern European company's phase III HIV vaccine trial among people who inject drugs in a South-East Asian country, with the company providing vaccine, research costs and laboratory equipment and local ethics committees approving it. An AIDS activist publication condemned the trial for not offering state-of-the-art treatment to participants who became HIV-positive, arguing that the country was chosen because its guidelines did not require it.

Gives the company's reply that state-of-the-art treatment would be unsustainable locally and an undue inducement, then asks whether the trial was ethical, whether a compromise exists, whether the gifts of equipment were appropriate and whether a local sponsor would be judged differently.

Case 33 describes how a European antiretroviral given as a single dose to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission was endorsed by WHO after a southern African study, though the data had not met good clinical practice standards and European regulators had not approved it. An East African regulator first refused approval but gave way under international pressure, and the case asks about the roles of the regulator and WHO.

Case 34 revisits quinacrine for non-surgical female sterilization in developing countries, with footnotes on terms and a link to Case 22. It explains women's limited access to contraception and surgical sterilization, the controversy over intrauterine quinacrine, and a non-governmental organization's 1990 withdrawal over cancer concerns after a cluster of cases in South America.

Describes how a report on over 30 000 women sterilized with quinacrine in South-East Asia led health organizations to advise against its use pending further studies, and how women's groups questioned the ethics of testing it without adequate toxicology data or informed choice. Questions ask whether double standards for contraceptive safety are ever acceptable and who should decide.

Case 35 describes a multi-site microbicide trial in East African family planning clinics, offering participants free STI care, Pap smears and treatment of unrelated illness that ordinary clinic users cannot afford, with footnotes on Pap smears and microbicides. It notes the protocol does not say whether this care will continue after the three-year trial. An ethics committee member and a community advisory board worry that women may join mainly to obtain health services, and the questions ask about undue inducement and whether the trial should go ahead.
A divider page for Chapter 6, on obligations to participants and communities.

Opens the Chapter 6 introduction on how far the obligations of researchers and sponsors extend, describing research as a partnership whose expectations should be agreed at the outset, especially where health care is lacking. It lists areas of possible obligation, such as care needed for the condition studied, and care and compensation for participants harmed during research.

Continues the list of possible obligations, covering continued access to effective treatment after a trial ends and care for health needs unrelated to the research. It discusses the limited view that consent and malpractice law cover researchers' duties, which depends on accessible health and justice systems.

Contrasts a narrow view of the researcher-participant relationship, limited to research roles, with a view of researchers as clinicians owing broader care to participants and possibly their families and communities. It warns that heavy community obligations could make research unaffordable and notes that ethics committees must decide how involved to be.

Explains that the role of ethics committees in negotiating benefits depends on their authority and whether communities can organize to negotiate. A recommended reading list follows, summarizing articles on ownership of human tissue inventions in developing countries and on condom provision and counselling in microbicide trials.

Continues the Chapter 6 reading list, summarizing articles arguing for providing full standards of care to participants in HIV prevention research in poor countries and for criteria on post-trial access to beneficial interventions.

Case 36, based on a 1970s study, explains the global burden of cervical cancer, with footnotes on Pap smears, dysplasia and squamous lesions. It describes a long-term observational study that screened women at eight public hospitals and followed those with abnormal smears, while treatment at the regional cancer centre usually involved a six-month wait. Because most women were illiterate, researchers gave simple explanations and obtained oral consent.

Explains that women were not told their lesions could become cancer or that treatment existed, and were followed every three months until carcinoma in situ, with delays in treatment. The study continued after a North American study showed all dysplasia needs treatment, and 71 women developed cancer; questions ask about duties to treat, interim review, stopping rules and publication.

Case 37 describes a multinational company's planned placebo-controlled trial of a malaria vaccine for infants in an East African village with intense transmission, with footnotes on anaemia and chloroquine resistance. It outlines recruitment through a maternal and child health clinic with busy nurses helping to translate, and vaccine doses given alongside routine immunizations. Children with malaria would be treated with chloroquine under national guidelines, and cases would be detected through an existing passive system.

Describes how health ministry representatives judged the consent process inadequate given low female literacy, and demanded free vaccination for all the country's children for five years if the vaccine works, which the company rejected. Questions cover the ethical issues, use of clinic staff for consent and obligations to the wider population.

Case 38 explains that refugees' mental health needs are often unmet and describes a European university clinic planning research among internally displaced people in a South-East Asian country to develop a culturally appropriate PTSD diagnostic scale, with a footnote defining PTSD. The study would be based at a village health centre where a psychiatrist visits only monthly. Community health workers paid per visit would introduce and translate, and ethnographers would collect contextual data.

Describes the anonymous one-hour interviews about violence and trauma, with oral consent and referral of those at high risk to government health centres, but no care provided by the study. Questions ask whether an ethics committee concerned about emotional distress should approve it, how risks and benefits balance, whether results should be returned and whether researchers should improve the referral services.

Case 39 describes a West African medical university and North American epidemiologists planning a community study of rotavirus incidence among children under two in a crowded city of about two million. It lists extra services that would be offered during the study, such as care for other illnesses, monthly malaria prophylaxis and transport costs, all ending when the study finishes.

The end of Case 39, asking how free care and transport might affect mothers' decisions and study results, whether services should continue afterwards and whether researchers must ensure results reach health planning.

Case 40 describes a South-East Asian research institute's planned trial of a new vaccine against cholera strain O139 among children under five in a rural area with a poorly equipped public clinic, comparing it with tetanus toxoid, explained in a footnote. The institute decides to provide state-of-the-art treatment for cholera and other diarrhoea at the site. Because it relies on grants, staff worry about promising long-term care it cannot afford, and the questions ask who should pay.
The end of Case 40, asking what information or action should accompany the vaccine and whether participants and other citizens should receive it free if it works.

Case 41 describes a health ministry team in a sub-Saharan African country studying how armed conflict has affected the health system, using focus groups with internally displaced and local people and interviews with leaders and officials. Community leaders would recruit participants and officials would pass on results, and the questions ask whether this is appropriate.

Case 42 describes a South Asian farming district where tribal people make up most of the landless poor and are excluded from local politics, and a study of willingness to pay for health services. During a gastroenteritis outbreak in a tribal village, young field researchers were accused by a local leader of colluding with non-tribal elites and favouring privatization.

Describes how the field team found that tribal people made up under 10% of focus group participants, mostly those receiving government aid, but the study leader dismissed their concerns. Questions ask who represents a diverse community, how to include minority views and what sponsors owe.

Case 43 describes a South Asian national programme giving US$100 a year per disabled child for community-based education services, with funds allocated using census data that missed many children. An evaluation expert found systematic bias, but an administrator urged him not to publicize it, arguing that including more severely disabled children would divert resources.

The end of Case 43, asking whether the researcher is right to insist on disclosure, whether an ethics committee should have reviewed the evaluation, and who bears most risk in health system evaluations.

Case 44 describes a large 1990s trial of an immune-modifying add-on drug for HIV in about 2500 people at 77 US centres, funded by a company that owned the data but agreed not to restrict publication. When the trial was stopped early for lack of benefit, the company demanded its own analyses be included and publications approved, so the researchers published using most of the data and were then sued. Questions ask who should own research data and whether sponsors may block publication.

Case 45 describes a small, genetically homogeneous island nation with a monarchy and a growing democracy movement, where diabetes prevalence has doubled to about 18%. A European biotechnology company announced a deal with the government to collect samples from families with diabetes, offering funds, a research centre and royalties. Community groups, the democracy movement and churches objected to the lack of public debate, privacy risks to relatives, patenting of life forms and meagre benefits, and the company withdrew.

The end of Case 45, asking whether groups have collective ownership of their genes, how governments should decide on genetic research, how to judge benefit sharing and whether a non-profit sponsor would change the ethics.
A divider page for Chapter 7, on privacy and confidentiality.

Opens the Chapter 7 introduction on who controls access to information, explaining that research can threaten privacy and confidentiality and that ethics committees must weigh potential harms against the value of knowledge. It discusses how to define the interests at stake. It notes that people's attitudes to secrecy vary, and defines confidentiality as a duty not to disclose information shared within a relationship.

Explains why doctors keep patient information confidential and gives examples of tangible harms from disclosure, such as revealing that a husband is not a child's father or that a man carries the Huntington disease gene. It notes that privacy matters even when no tangible interest is at stake. It also observes that research using information from public sources poses special challenges.

Explains that electronic records, genetic databases and online data mean individuals are losing control over information about their health, and that cheap genome sequencing will permanently identify people and their relatives. It acknowledges the benefits such resources bring, such as finding genetic susceptibilities and drug side-effects. A recommended reading list begins with an article on disclosing research results to participants.
Continues the Chapter 7 reading list, summarizing articles on researchers' duty to share results with participants and on how data protection law affects public health practice.

Case 46 describes a West African study of nevirapine given to HIV-positive women at delivery and to their newborns to reduce transmission, with test results promised to be kept confidential. A woman who tested positive, the fourth wife of an older man, disclosed other sexual partners, and the doctor felt he should tell the husband, while colleagues disagreed; questions ask whether confidentiality may be broken.

Case 47 describes a university evaluation, funded by a European university, of care quality in a South Asian family welfare programme, under an ethics committee's advice to conceal the identity of primary health centres and staff. A field researcher saw a health worker reusing syringes, reported it anonymously to a supervisor, and saw it happen again a week later. Questions ask whether confidentiality should be strictly kept and what the study leader should do.

Case 48 describes the same kind of evaluation, in which researchers who had promised anonymity reported to officials that some primary health centres and sterilization camps gave poor care. When officials demanded the centres' names, accused the researchers of fabrication and argued confidentiality did not protect wrongdoers, the researchers refused; questions ask when confidentiality should be upheld.

Case 49 describes a non-governmental group's community-based study of complications after abortion in 140 villages of an Eastern European country, where many abortions occur outside approved centres. It explains that women would be recruited through abortion providers and community health workers and interviewed at home. To prevent stigma, interviews would be disguised by also holding dummy interviews with women who had not had abortions.

Describes further measures to protect women in the abortion study, such as focusing questions on gynaecological history and using dummy interviews with family members, and a funder ethics committee member's worry about leaks of identifying records. Questions ask for comment on these protections and whether recruitment was free of coercion.

Case 50 describes a Central American mental health institute that funds long-term care at community mental health centres and wants to assess its cost-effectiveness using confidential psychiatric records. It would reimburse care only for patients who consent to release their records, which some clinicians call coercive, and the questions ask when a state agency may access personal records.

Case 51 describes a proposed study of genetic links between brainwave patterns and alcoholism among a North American indigenous people, paying 300 families about US$300 each. A tribal body urged the ethics committee to reject it, citing lack of consultation, the sacredness of blood and the risk of stigma, and the questions ask how the committee should respond.

Case 52 describes a proposed telephone case-control study of vasectomy and prostate cancer in an industrialized country, with controls drawn from the electoral register. The researchers would not tell participants the study's purpose, fearing biased answers, and the questions ask whether oral consent and withholding the hypothesis are acceptable.

Case 53 describes social scientists who used hospital records to visit, without prior permission, women with abnormal Pap smears who had not returned for their results, to learn how to improve services. Questions ask whether this breached confidentiality, whether they should give the women their results and what alternatives existed.

Case 54 describes a large southern African farm employing seasonal workers, where men far outnumber women in the compounds and many migrant men live without partners. It recounts how health promotion researchers presented their survey to management and workers, clarified that they were not advocates, and mapped contacts between workers and local communities. They found sexual contact between local girls, some under 15, and migrant men, raising concern about HIV and other STIs.

The end of Case 54, asking whether researchers should tell management about under-age girls working on the farm, whether they must try to protect them, and which actions are duties versus morally permissible.

Case 55 describes a survey of reproductive health risks among girls aged 13–17 working as domestic servants away from their families in sub-Saharan Africa, many recruited through trafficking disguised as fostering. Interviewers would seek household permission, get the child's signed consent, interview privately with a decoy questionnaire, and offer contacts and small payments. The questions ask about privacy, safety, who should consent and whether former child workers could be studied instead.
A divider page for Chapter 8, on professional ethics.

Opens the Chapter 8 introduction on divided loyalties to science and on defining and regulating research misconduct, listing reasonable expectations of integrity such as no fabrication or plagiarism, accurate reporting and full conflict of interest disclosures. It begins discussing conflicts of interest, giving the example of a journal editor who consults for a drug company.

Discusses conflicts of interest, noting that holding potentially conflicting roles is not wrong in itself, and distinguishes them from conflicts of mission between patient care and science discussed in Chapter 1. It explains how commercial biotechnology funding and scientists' financial ties to companies have made such conflicts more common. It also notes that community leaders may have hidden interests that ethics committees find hard to detect.

Notes that ethics committee members may also have conflicts of interest and need disclosure and recusal policies, since their primary duty is to protect participants. It then defines scientific misconduct using the Wellcome Trust description of fabrication, falsification, plagiarism and deception. It cites a US survey in which under 2% of scientists admitted serious misconduct, while many admitted lesser lapses.

Raises the ethical questions in responding to misconduct, such as who should investigate, protect wrongly accused scientists and shield whistle-blowers, and whether views of misconduct differ across cultures. It lists measures such as data monitoring, trial registration and independent access to raw data. A recommended reading list begins with articles on conflicts of interest in drug trials and industry ties of review board members.

Continues the Chapter 8 reading list, summarizing studies on financial ties between review board members and industry, on whistle-blowing and scientific misconduct, and on ethical research across cultures.

Case 56 describes a manufacturer-funded trial comparing a new hormonal contraceptive given by pill, skin patch or injection in two socioeconomic groups of women, in which the company paid local researchers' salaries, gave each a computer and paid about US$1000 per completed volunteer. Participants stopped their usual contraception and received small compensation for failures or side-effects, and the questions ask whether these benefits are appropriate.

Case 57 describes an Asian company that, after regulators refused approval of a schizophrenia drug because some trial participants developed heart rhythm problems, contracted an Eastern European psychiatric hospital with long-stay, rarely visited patients to run further trials. Patients were told only that the drug might slightly affect heart activity, and regulators there were not told of the Asian decision; questions ask about risks, benefits and disclosure.

Case 58 describes an ethics committee at a South-East Asian national university medical school that refused to review a North American university's US$500 000-a-year family planning study unless it saw the budget. The North American side feared the 10% overhead would bias the committee, while the committee argued budget review was essential to judge feasibility and local benefit.

Case 59 describes a West African mining company's employee welfare group asking a European university team to estimate the economic cost of the HIV epidemic to the workforce, hoping to persuade management to fund prevention. The study is fully funded by the company, which requires anonymity but does not restrict publication. The case then describes the composition of the research team.

Lists the team's findings that HIV could cause at least 10% staff turnover and that medical costs could reach 15% of operating costs, recommending home-based treatment and prevention. The company president warned that paying for all HIV care would force closure or relocation and asked the team to recommend limited insurance coverage instead, raising questions about researchers' independence.

Case 60 describes a small non-governmental organization working in a South Asian slum that partnered with a research institute to study how forced resettlement affected people's health, education and livelihoods. The ethics committee ruled that selecting case studies from the organization's clinic patients was unethical, as they might feel care depended on taking part. The organization disagreed, arguing clinic patients would give richer information than randomly chosen respondents.

The end of Case 60, noting the organization felt the study no longer served its advocacy aims, and asking whether the committee's decision was justified and how to balance research with the need for action.

Case 61 describes a research assistant who found that a prominent senior researcher had altered data to fit his hypothesis on lipids and cardiovascular disease. A former colleague warned her that everyone could be harmed and she would need solid proof, since the researcher brought in large grants. After finding further signs of falsified data, she filed a formal complaint of scientific misconduct.

Gives the senior researcher's defence that pressure to bring in grant money, responsibility for his lab members and a desire to serve the community led him to falsify data, and asks whether these reasons are valid, how whistle-blowers should be treated and who is responsible for scientific integrity.

Case 62 describes six genetics graduate students who came to suspect their professor of falsifying data, including reusing published data as unpublished in grant applications. She blamed computer errors, and the students worried about their own work, including one who could not reproduce earlier results. They faced a collective decision on whether to report her, knowing their degrees could be delayed.
The end of Case 62, asking whether the students should report the professor, what happens if they stay silent, and what the university owes to whistle-blowers.

Case 63 describes Dr Taylor, a renowned nutrition and immunology expert at a North American university, who ran an infant formula allergy study for a drug company while his nurse struggled to recruit participants. When he published results of another company's formula study that seemed impossible to have recruited for, the company's research associate challenged him. He also published a third formula study, raising doubts about how so many infants were enrolled.

Recounts how the university, fearing lawsuits, did not pursue the allegations firmly, while Taylor continued publishing, including a multivitamin study a journal rejected as likely fabricated after he could not produce data, which another journal then published. It notes he later published supporting work in his own journal, including a paper by an author who could not be traced.
The end of Case 63, with questions on the roles of governments, professional societies and journals in dealing with scientific fraud.

Case 64 describes a prolific Central American researcher who, after leaving an institute, was asked by a funder to review a proposal by a well-known researcher in another country that turned out to copy his own unfunded proposal. The funder rejected it but asked him to keep the matter confidential, which he was unwilling to accept.

The end of Case 64, with questions on which ethical standards researchers should follow, whether ideas in a proposal belong to their author and for how long, and whether former collaborators must include a departed colleague in later funding and publications.

Part of the list of recommended resources, describing training and capacity-building initiatives such as the bilingual TRREE programme for research ethics in Africa and UNESCO's bioethics activities, including its Global Ethics Observatory, among others.

Part of the recommended reading list, describing guidance documents such as the US National Bioethics Advisory Commission report on clinical trials in developing countries and UNAIDS/WHO guidance on HIV prevention trials.
Part of the recommended reading list, describing documents such as the UNESCO International Declaration on Human Genetic Data and WHO guidance on ethics.
Part of the recommended reading list, describing WHO operational guidelines for ethics committees reviewing biomedical research and other literature on ethics committees in developing countries.
Part of the recommended reading list on ethics committees, including articles on building ethical review capacity in developing countries and on for-profit ethics review boards.
Part of the recommended reading list, including an article on how political and human rights contexts affect research ethics review, and work on what makes clinical research ethical.
Part of the recommended reading list, including an article on the blurred line between audit and research and other chapter readings.

Part of the chapter-by-chapter reading list, covering readings for the chapters on study design and on harms and benefits, such as articles on exclusion of older people from studies and scientific imperialism.
Part of the chapter-by-chapter reading list on informed consent, including articles on consent in developing countries and clinical trials.
Part of the reading list on informed consent and standards of care, including experience obtaining consent for a vaccine trial in rural Senegal and the FDA response to the Declaration of Helsinki.
Part of the reading list on obligations to participants and communities, including articles on ownership of human tissue inventions and standards of care in HIV prevention research.
Part of the reading list on standards of care and privacy, including articles on care obligations of rich-country sponsors and ethical challenges in community research.
Part of the reading list on professional ethics, including articles on conflicts of interest in drug trials and ethical research across cultures.

The start of the appendix, reprinting with permission the general ethical principles from the CIOMS/WHO International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects, beginning with respect for persons and the protection of vulnerable people.

Continues the CIOMS principles on justice, stating that research should not exploit poor countries and should leave them better off or no worse, respond to their health needs and make products reasonably available.
